But my father was with me, offering comfort and replacing painful memories with bright hopes. It almost seemed sweet to cry when he was there to dry my tears.

He also drew my thoughts away from my grief by comparing it with the despair he had felt when my mother died. Even then, his description of his emotions made me shudder. He had a poet's imagination, and when he spoke of the storm that had torn through him, his words brought it so vividly to life that I believed him and trembled. I wondered how he had ever returned to ordinary life after thoughts so wild seemed to have brought him close to another world. The ideas he expressed were so enormous that the human heart seemed too small to hold them. Such feelings seemed suited to a spirit living among earthquakes and volcanoes, rather than one enclosed in a human body and face. But those were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was entirely loving and gentle. When I looked up in wonder as he spoke, his smile assured me that only the tenderest feelings ruled his heart.

Two months after my aunt died, we moved to London. There my father encouraged me to study more deeply than I ever had before. My progress delighted him. He stayed with me through all my studies, helping or joining me in every lesson. We spent much time in company, and every day he tried to make life brighter with some fresh pleasure. His tender love for me, and the love and respect I felt for him, gave every moment its charm. The hours seemed long because we filled every minute. We experienced more in a week than many people do in several months, and the variety and freshness of our pleasures made each one more enjoyable.

We constantly went on outings together. Sometimes we visited beautiful scenery, sometimes we looked at fine paintings, and sometimes we simply went out in search of whatever amusement we might find. Whatever the purpose, I was always happy beside my father. Whenever someone else joined us, I felt disappointed. Yet if I turned toward him with an unhappy look, his eyes, fixed tenderly on mine, immediately restored my joy. Oh, those hours of intense delight! They were brief, yet looking back through the mist of sorrow that rose immediately afterward, as if to hide them from me, I feel that they lasted an entire lifetime.

Presently midnight sounded from the lofty Westminster tower, and the night appeared to quiver at every resonant stroke. The railway lights then vanished, leaving a single lamp shining like an immense ruby upon a towering mast, while the city's roar grew more distant.

At two he rose and wandered in the direction of Blackfriars. Everything seemed unreal, like some extraordinary dream. Across the river, the houses appeared fashioned from darkness. It was as though shadow and silver had made the world afresh. Through the dim air the great dome of St. Paul's rose like a bubble.

Nearing Cleopatra's Needle, he noticed a man bending over the parapet. As he approached, the man raised his head, and the gaslight struck his face directly.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! That plump, flaccid face, those gold-edged spectacles, the weak and sickly smile, the sensual lips—there could be no mistaking them.

Lord Arthur halted. A splendid thought darted through his mind, and he crept noiselessly behind the man. In an instant he grasped Mr. Podgers by his legs and pitched him into the Thames. A vulgar curse, a tremendous splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered over anxiously, but all he could see of the cheiromantist was a tall hat revolving in a moonlit eddy. Before long this, too, went under, leaving no visible sign of Mr. Podgers. Once he imagined he saw the heavy, ungainly body swimming towards the steps beside the bridge, and a dreadful sense of failure seized him. It proved to be only a reflection, disappearing when the moon emerged from behind a cloud. At last he seemed to have fulfilled destiny's decree. With a long sigh of relief, he whispered Sybil's name.

'Have you lost something, sir?' a voice abruptly asked behind him.

Turning, he found a policeman carrying a bull's-eye lantern.

'Nothing that matters, sergeant,' he replied with a smile. He hailed a passing hansom, sprang inside, and directed the driver to Belgrave Square.

Throughout the following days he passed repeatedly from hope to apprehension. At certain moments he almost expected Mr. Podgers to enter the room; at others, he believed Fate could never treat him so unfairly. Twice he visited the cheiromantist's address in West Moon Street, but could not summon the courage to ring. He yearned for certainty and dreaded it.

At last certainty arrived. He was taking tea in the club's smoking room, listening somewhat listlessly to Surbiton describe the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when a waiter appeared with the evening newspapers.

I rushed to her, caught her in my arms, and covered her with caresses, pleading:

"Tell me, darling, tell me! What has happened?"

Her head dropped helplessly against my chest, and she whispered in a barely audible gasp:

"HELLO-CENTRAL!"

"Hurry!" I cried to Clarence. "Telephone the king's homeopath and tell him to come!"

Within two minutes I was on my knees beside the child's crib, while Sandy sent servants flying in every direction throughout the palace. A glance was almost enough to show me the trouble—membranous croup! I stooped and murmured:

"Wake up, little sweetheart! Hello-Central."

Her gentle eyes opened wearily, and she managed to utter:

"Papa."

That heartened me. She was nowhere near dead yet. I ordered preparations of sulphur and fetched the croup-kettle myself; when Sandy or the child falls ill, I do not sit idle awaiting physicians. Experience had taught me how to nurse them both. This little creature had spent much of her brief existence in my arms, and I could frequently quiet her distress and make her smile through the tear-drops upon her lashes even when her mother could not.

Just then Sir Launcelot strode through the great hall in his finest armour, bound for the stock-board. He presided over that body and held the Siege Perilous, purchased from Sir Galahad; the board was composed of the Knights of the Round Table, who now employed their table for commercial affairs. Seats there fetched—well, the sum would defeat belief, so there is no point in giving it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, had established a corner in one of the new lines, and meant to squeeze the shorts that very day. But what did that matter? He remained the old Launcelot. One glance through the doorway as he passed, one discovery that his darling was ill, sufficed. Bulls and bears could settle their quarrel however they pleased; he would come in and give little Hello-Central every bit of help he could. And come in he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute had replaced the alcohol lamp's wick and was heating the croup-kettle. Sandy had meanwhile arranged a blanket tent above the crib, and all was prepared.

Sir Launcelot raised the steam. Together we charged the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a little lactic acid, filled it with water, and slipped the steam nozzle beneath the canopy. With everything now in proper order, we took our places on opposite sides of the crib and began our vigil.
